Items.Authors: Binbin Xiang, Shike Mo, XueTong Yang, Wei Wang, Longfei Niu
Items.Title: Fault diagnosis technique for radio telescope antenna drive reducer gears based on the fused model
Items.Abstract: Low-speed operation of antenna drive reducer gears suffers from reduced SNR, obscuring fault features under noise interference where traditional methods fail. This study proposes an RBMO-optimized SVMD-MCKD-CNN-LSTM fusion model (RSM-CL) for fault diagnosis. RBMO-optimized SVMD-MCKD first enhances raw signals via noise reduction and feature amplification. Subsequently, CNN extracts localized spatial features while LSTM captures temporal dependencies for deep fault characterization. Experimental validation demonstrates the model achieves >97% average classification accuracy, outperforming conventional single-decomposition/single-model approaches in both diagnostic precision and computational efficiency (reduced processing time). This framework establishes a novel solution for low-speed reducer gear fault diagnosis.

Items.Authors: Luke M. Schmidt, Hudson Malone, Noah Siebersma, Erika Cook, Jennifer L. Marshall, Darren L. DePoy, Ryan J. Oelkers, Silvana Delgado Andrade, Enrique Gonzalez Vega, Shravan Menon, Chelsea Taylor, Lars Walker
Items.Title: Fiber optic characterization for unprecedented sky subtraction (FOCUSS)
Items.Abstract: Future massively multiplexed astronomical spectroscopic surveys will require accurate and repeatable removal of  the sky background. The Fiber Optic Characterization for Unprecedented Sky Subtraction (FOCUSS) project  aims to automate the characterization of fiber optic cables in order to determine their throughput efficiency  and focal ratio degradation (FRD). The laboratory setup is useful for fiber optic selection, fiber optic assembly  verification, and potentially inform the development of telescope facility calibration systems. The throughput  efficiency measures the fiber transmission as a function of wavelength, while the FRD test measures the angular  spread of light exiting the test fiber as a function of incident angle. FOCUSS operates between 350-1000 nm and  uses the Python programming language for data collection, reduction, and analysis.

Items.Authors: Valentina Viotto, Alessandro Ballone, Davide Greggio, Luca Marafatto, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Andrea Baruffolo, Maria Bergomi, Elena Carolo, Simonetta Chinellato, Simone Di Filippo, Marco Dima, Jacopo Farinato, Demetrio Magrin, Lorenzo Merli, Roberto Ragazzoni, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Kalyan Kumar Radhakrishnan Santhakumari, Daniele Vassallo, David Barr, Sylvain Cetre, Gabriele Umbriaco
Items.Title: Final design of the MATTO test bench
Items.Abstract: The MATTO test bench, under development at INAF-OAPD, is a multi-purpose wide-field AO test facility, whose opto-mechanical design is aimed at simulating existing or future MCAO systems configurations with test or validation purposes. It will allow exploring a wide range of WFSs and sources combinations, thanks to the modularity of its design. It includes a reference source module, which simulates the atmospheric behaviour on natural and laser guide stars, a telescope simulator module, a MCAO correction module, allowing to mimic a number of optical configurations in which three DMs can be independently conjugated at various distances, and a sensing module, which allows to replicate the main properties of different types of WFSs. The DAO4MATTO Real-Time Control system, based on the DAO software solution, will provide MCAO loop control, keeping the system’s modular approach, for all possible configurations.

Items.Authors: Charlotte E. Guthery, Jacob Taylor, Mahawa Cisse, Scott Lilley, Eduardo Marin, Jonathan Steiner, Avinash Surendran, Edward Wetherell, Peter Wizinowich, Tatum Umiamaka, Marcos van Dam, Sylvain Cetre, Mike Bottom, Maria Vincent, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Maissa Salama, Mayra Gutierrez, Antonin Bouchez
Items.Title: First on-sky results of the HAKA deformable mirror upgrade
Items.Abstract: For the first time in 25 years, Keck Observatory has upgraded one of its deformable mirrors (DM) as a part of the High-order Advanced Keck Adaptive optics (HAKA) project. The 349-actuator Xinetics DM was replaced with a state of the art 2844-actuator ALPAO DM. During this install, the Shack-Hartmann Wavefront Sensor (SHWFS) was upgraded to match the higher density actuators with new 57x57 high-order and 26x26 low-order lenslet array. Along with the hardware changes, the calibration and operational software for the AO system was upgraded to a more modular and user-friendly Python interface.  These upgrades have shown a major improvement to the Keck II on-sky performance. Previously, performance was dominated by fitting error and the DM stroke saturated during poor conditions. The new DM shows consistently better performance on the same targets and during high seeing. These first light results will pave the way to improved science and high contrast observing on the Keck II telescope.

Items.Authors: Thomas Granzer, Jörg Weingrill, Arto Järvinen, Klaus Strassmeier
Items.Title: First results of a continuous monitoring campaign of the PLATO Southern field
Items.Abstract: The BMK10k is a 35cm refracting telescope on a German equatorial mount. It  is located at the National Observatory of the Polish Academy of Sciences close to ESO's ELT.   It offers an incredibly large field of view of 52.5 square degrees on a 10k  detector, with a sampling rate of 2.5"/pixel. The telescope has a  single filter Johnson V filter. It is intended for ground-based support for the PLATO mission of ESA.   The entire telescope and dome are fully robotic and run on a clone of the  STELLA control software. The schedule is extremely simple. Cycle through the 3x3  fields at the optimal airmass and ensure the same number of observations are made in each field.   For each field, take three consecutive exposures of 60 seconds.   In July and August 2025, we obtained an almost continuous dataset spanning 40 days.  More than 10 million stars were identified and their light curves could be retrieved.   This poster shows example light curves alongside a brief description of the telescope.

Items.Authors: Christopher Foster, Charles White, Kevin Kady, Christian Guerra, Christopher Sanchez
Items.Title: FMS programming lessons learned
Items.Abstract: The controls of the U.S. National Science Foundations’s (NSF) Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) Facility Management System (FMS) have evolved with continuous improvement based upon the needs over the telescope’s evolution. The FMS is the system that controls the thermal operations. The FMS controls have evolved and changed as the needs of the telescope have changed and as lessons were learned. As the telescope moved from operational commissioning to operations, there was an opportunity to engage an outside consulting firm to engage in a thorough review of the entire thermal system both to gain perspective on the overall design as well as to check for potential energy savings and improved operations. The engineering firm Burns & McDonnell was hired to work with involved DKIST employees to perform this review. This paper is a review of the lessons learned during commissioning of the FMS as well as the results and recommendations from the consultation.

Items.Authors: Valentin Sauvage, Nabila Aghanim, Anaïs Besnard, Ivan Charles, Clémence de Jabrun, Jean-Marc Duval, Bruno Maffei, Sylvain Martin, Bruno Borgo
Items.Title: FOSSIL's preliminary thermal architecture
Items.Abstract: The FOSSIL mission, proposed to ESA’s M8 call, aims to achieve unprecedented measurements of CMB spectral distortions and therefore requires an exceptionally stable cryogenic environment. Its payload features a dual-input, dual-output FTS and four FPUs operating from 50 to 2000 GHz, all mounted on a 4.5 K actively cooled bench. The thermal architecture combines passive radiative cooling with a 4.5 K cooler delivering 50 mW. Sub-Kelvin temperatures are provided by a multi-stage ADR offering continuous cooling at 1.8 K and 350 mK, and a final stage at 50 mK for the FPUs. This configuration ensures the stability needed for high-precision spectral-distortion measurements.

Items.Authors: V. Conforti, G. Tosti, V. Pastore, P. Bruno, S. Germani, G. Giavitto, S. Iovenitti, N. La Palombara, A. Marchetti, C. Molfese, E. Rol, A. Sulich, A. Trois, V. Voitsekhovskyi, J. Watson, R. White
Items.Title: From design to verification: applying the software quality and test plans to the SST telescope control system for CTA
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is the next-generation facility for very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy, featuring arrays of telescopes of different sizes at two sites. The Small-Sized Telescopes (SSTs), deployed in Chile, will explore the highest energies up to 300 TeV. Each SST is managed by a Telescope Control System (TCS) that coordinates all subsystems and interfaces with the central Array Control and Data Acquisition system. The project is currently finalizing the preparation for the Test Readiness Review planned for late 2025. This paper describes how the TCS Software Quality Assurance and Test Plans are applied to guide this phase, including continuous integration, automated testing, and hardware-in-the-loop validation. The structured quality process enhances maturity, traceability, and risk control, supporting readiness for formal verification and establishing consistent software standards across CTAO.

Items.Authors: Windell Tanaka, Milan Štubljar
Items.Title: From geometry to efficiency: updated CFHT astrometric camera pointing model and estimated on-sky time savings
Items.Abstract: We present an updated geometric pointing model for the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) astrometric camera using an expanded on-sky dataset. The model treats the equatorial (HA–Dec) mount and camera as a rigid 3-D system that maps encoder angles to focal-plane coordinates via a set of rotations and translations. Building on our earlier solution, we refit encoder zero points, axis tilts, non-perpendicularity, camera collimation offsets, and gravity-dependent flexure using fields spanning a wider range of hour angle, declination, rotator angle, and conditions. We quantify residuals across the focal plane, test parameter stability, and compare performance with the previous model using independent validation fields. The updated solution reduces blind pointing errors and systematic trends, particularly at high airmass. We estimate on-sky time savings from fewer acquisition dithers needed to place targets at the desired focal-plane location.

Items.Authors: Giovanna Jerse, Kamal Sant, Mariarita Murabito, Lidia Contarino, Fabiana Ferrente, Fabrizio Giorgi, Dario Del Moro, Teodora Mihailescu, Roberto Cirami, Ilaria Ermolli
Items.Title: From IDL to Python: A modular, standards-compliant re-engineering of the IBIS2.0 Data-Reduction Pipeline
Items.Abstract: The IBIS2.0 Python Pipeline: Modernizing Solar Spectro-Polarimetry. IBIS2.0, the upgraded Interferometric Bidimensional Spectrometer, is relocating to the THEMIS solar telescope with a modernized optical system. This requires a complete re-engineering of the calibration and data-reduction pipeline, migrating from legacy IDL code to a modern, fully Python-based architecture. The new pipeline preserves core physics while greatly enhancing robustness, reproducibility, and long-term maintainability. Its modular structure is user-friendly, fully compatible with modern workflow orchestrators and ensures seamless integration with the SunPy ecosystem. This advancement enables automated, standards-compliant and scalable production of calibrated IBIS2.0 data. We present the key architectural developments, revised calibration procedures and the implications for scientific exploitation.

Items.Authors: Edison Bustos, Guillermo Damke, Steve Heathcote, Andrei Tokovinin
Items.Title: Fully automated system for real-time remote site testing deployed at Cerro Morado, Chile
Items.Abstract: Cerro Morado (2,100 m), located between Cerro Tololo and Cerro Pachón in Chile, is being evaluated as a potential site for future astronomical facilities. An autonomous monitoring system was deployed, including a RINGSS seeing monitor, a full-parameter weather station, and SQM-LE/TESS-W4C photometers for multi-band sky-brightness characterization. The installation is powered by a 3 kW photovoltaic system optimized for high-altitude operation and connected to the CTIO network via a wireless link, enabling real-time data transfer and remote system monitoring. Telemetry is archived on CTIO servers, where automated pipelines perform quality control and generate science-ready products. Initial results indicate stable seeing and dark-sky conditions comparable to other high-quality sites in northern Chile. The design and implementation have been made available for the community.

Items.Authors: Camilo E. Jiménez Ángel, Ditte Slumstrup, Antonio L. Cabrera Lavers, Daniel Reverte Payá, José A. Rodríguez Losada, Víctor Rodríguez Herreros, Juan J. Fernández-Valdivia, Alfonso G. Cardell Bilbao
Items.Title: Fully Autonomous Data Processing for the GTC: The DRAGO System
Items.Abstract: The DRAGO system is a fully automated platform that executes the Data Reduction Process (DRP) for all GTC instruments without human intervention. It transforms raw data into standardized scientific products through automated orchestration, intelligent workflow management, and robust reprocessing. DRAGO is DRP-agnostic, integrating pipelines in any format or programming language. Its core functions include automatic observing block detection, calibration management, autonomous DRP configuration, and standardized output generation. These operate within a scalable architecture featuring data management, process scheduling, automatic quality control, and a user interface with API access. DRAGO enables fast, reliable, and reproducible reductions, representing a major step toward fully autonomous data handling in modern observatories.

Items.Authors: Haeun Chung, Carlos Vargas, Erika Hamden
Items.Title: GlowSat: a CubeSat mission concept for far-UV airglow line distribution mapping
Items.Abstract: GlowSat is a Far-Ultraviolet (FUV) 6U CubeSat mission concept designed to map the distribution of FUV airglow lines between 101 nm and 141 nm in the Earth’s upper atmosphere. Understanding the temporal and spatial behavior of these bright FUV airglow background lines is essential for planning future astrophysical FUV missions in low-Earth orbit (LEO), particularly for detecting faint diffuse emissions from the circumgalactic and intergalactic media. GlowSat will determine the correlation between airglow-line intensity and both solar activity and the spacecraft’s viewing geometry and attitude. These relationships will provide a baseline reference for all future FUV observations from LEO. GlowSat employs a compact 2U-size FUV spectrograph payload with Si E-beam lithography grating and a commercial CMOS sensor with a scintillator coating. This presentation highlights the science motivation and mission design of the GlowSat mission concept.

Items.Authors: Arend Moerman, Nikita A. Soshnin, Stefanie A. Brackenhoff, Kenichi Karatsu, Louis H. Marting, Steven A. de Rooij, Bernhard R. Brandl, Akira Endo
Items.Title: GPU-accelerated observational forecasting of superconducting (sub)millimeter integral field units
Items.Abstract: Scientific interpretation of data obtained with superconducting (sub)millimeter integral field units (IFUs) requires careful design of reduction and analysis pipelines. However, the quality and behavior of the designed pipelines must be assessed before they are applied, requiring simulated observational data.  To this end, we have developed GATEAU, a GPU-accelerated software framework for simulating realistic (sub)millimeter observations of arbitrary astronomical sources with IFUs using MKIDs. The framework consists of a Python interface powered by a C/C++ backend, which achieves GPU-acceleration through Nvidia’s CUDA library. The output is stored in FITS format, which the user can feed to their pipeline.  We present the software implementation of GATEAU and several comparisons between GATEAU and on-sky DESHIMA 2.0 data, serving as validation tests. Finally, we present a use case focusing on the TIFUUN instrument, illustrating the kind of analysis that can be done with GATEAU.

Items.Authors: V. Gopinath, E. Aller Carpentier, F. Allouche, M. Baeten, H. Bedigan, J. Beltran, A. Berdeu, G. Bourdarot, C. Cárdenas, M. Comin, H. Cristian, D. Del Valle, F. Delplancke-Ströbele, F. Eisenhauer, B. Ernstberger, L. Esteras Otal, C. Fruck, E. Fuentesca, F. Gonté, J. Graf, P. Gutierrez Cheetham, R. Guzman Collazos, W. Hackenberg, F. Haussmann, R. Holzlöhner, K. Holzner, S. Huber, F. Kamphues, J. Kolb, P. Krempl, JB. Le Bouquin, I. Maria Guidolin, S. Menéndez Mendoza, S. Oberti, L. Pallanca, F. Pedreros Bustos, R. Pohl, D. Popovic, C. Rau, C. Reinero, M. Riquelme, C. Rose, M. Scherbarth, R. Schwerdt, B. Speet, A. Urban, G. Zins
Items.Title: GRAVITY+ LGS (laser guide star): assembly, integration, and verification at the Very Large Telescope
Items.Abstract: A major infrastructure upgrade to the Very Large Telescope interferometer (VLTI) was done by the consortia led project GRAVITY+. GRAVITY+ aims to significantly improve the sensitivity, sky coverage and contrast for milliarcsecond interferometry. As part of the upgrade, new adaptive optics (4 Shack Hartmann Wavefront Sensors + 4 Deformable Mirrors+ 4 new Real Time Computers) were installed in August 2024 at all 4 Unit Telescopes (UTs). The last part of the upgrade consisted of the installation of Laser Guide Star Units (LGSU) in UTs' 1, 2 and 3 (UT4 is already equipped with 4 LGSUs'). Three LGSUs' were tested at the ESO headquarters in Garching, and were shipped to Paranal in early June 2025. With a large team of engineers from ESO, the GRAVITY+ consortia and contractors, a successful Assembly, Integration and Verification phase (AIV) was carried out between August to October 2025.

Items.Authors: Hannah C. Gulick, Shunsaku Nagasawa, Koothodil Abhijith Augustine, Melodi Ebrahimi, Mathew Dexter, Josh Forgione, Hannah Goldberg, Nihal Gulati, Sarah Jauregui, Andrew Ji, Chris Moeckel, Aldo Aguilar-Nadalini, Kazuhiro Nakazawa, Keigo Okuma, Srisha Rewatkar, Isabel Schmidtke, Andreas Zoglauer, Tadayuki Takahashi, Juan Carlos Martinez Oliveros, John Tomsick
Items.Title: Ground calibration of the Background and Transient Observer (BTO) gamma-ray instrument on COSI
Items.Abstract: The Background and Transient Observer (BTO) is a soft gamma-ray instrument that will fly on NASA’s Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) mission in 2027. BTO is a Student Collaboration project that consists of two NaI(Tl) detectors, SiPM readouts, and custom electronics, providing spectra and light curves in the 30 keV to 2 MeV range. BTO has two primary science goals: detect astrophysical transients and monitor the soft gamma-ray background.     In this talk, I will present the comprehensive ground calibration campaign undertaken to prepare BTO for flight, including system characterization and environmental qualification. The results from these tests verify instrument robustness and characterize the expected on-orbit performance. Finally, I will discuss how the calibration results map onto BTO’s science capabilities, including transient sensitivity, background modeling accuracy, and expected on-orbit performance within the COSI mission.

Items.Authors: Corentin Cudennec, Alexandre Jeanneau, Roland Bacon, Thierry Lépine, Matthew Lehnert, Rémi Giroud, Jean-Emmanuel Migniau, David Lee, Roelof S. de Jong, Laurane Fréour
Items.Title: Guiding design choices for wide-field IFS: trade-off between replication and complexity for WST
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a proposed 12-meter segmented telescope optimized for seeing-limited observations in the visible. It is designed for the simultaneous operation of a high-multiplex multi-object spectrograph (30,000 fibers) and a large panoramic integral field spectrograph (3×3 arcmin). This paper presents the integrated design approach adopted for the IFS, focusing on a trade study of spectrograph architectures. We explore design choices such as pixel pitch, detector format, and camera optical design against throughput, image quality, error budgets, volume, cost, and image slicer geometry. The study adds one ecological metric: the CO₂ footprint of building each spectrograph, to inform design sustainability. The study also explores the potential of curved detectors, which can improve aberration control and throughput. Early results suggest that many simpler spectrographs outperform fewer complex units technically and economically.

Items.Authors: John Nijim, Zoran Ninkov, Dmitry Vorobiev, Aditya Kinjawadekar
Items.Title: Hadamard Transform Spectral Imaging (HTSI): Dealing with incomplete data and optimizing masks
Items.Abstract: Hadamard Transform Spectral Imaging (HTSI) is a signal multiplexing technique used to obtain spectra at every spatial point in the field of view of an instrument, similar to an Integral Field Unit (IFU) spectrograph. Its main advantage is to provide a signal-to-noise (SNR) increase over direct measurements within the same observation time, where the multiplex advantage is realized. Instruments equipped with micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) such as digital micromirror devices (DMDs) or micro-shutter arrays (MSAs) can implement the masks efficiently, and HTSI can be an observing mode in upcoming astrophysics space-based missions with instruments that use MEMS devices, such as CASTOR and HWO. In this study, an alternative to the inverse Hadamard transform is implemented, by use of a total variation inverse regularization problem with compressive sensing, and methods are explored which reduce the SNR degradation of weaker signals due to Poisson photon noise from stronger signals.

Items.Authors: Kjetil Dohlen, David Le Mignant, Anne Bonnefoi, Marc Dubbeldam, Johan Floriot, Iago Funes Vecino, Laurent Jocou, Yoann Richaud, Alexis Carlotti, Zalpha Challita, Anne Costille, Andrew Dunn, David King, Deborah Malone, Guillermo Mercant Rubio, Timothy Morris, Jean-François Sauvage, Lazar Staykov, Teodora Aleida Viera-Curbelo
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: reoptimization of the natural guide star sensors (NGSS) system for MCAO compatibility
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from below 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. This paper describes the impact on the natural guide star sensors (NGSS) system of the rescope of the instrument involving going behind the MORFEO MCAO system, Wide-ranging changes have been imposed in particular to the low-order wavefront sensors (LOWFS) previously optimized for LTAO operation, as well as on the external support and enclosure (ESE) whose external interfaces have changed. The high-contrast module (HCM) is also deeply affected due to the modified plate scale of the instrument, and the single-conjucate AO sensor (SCAOS) benefits from a reduced patrol field requirement

Items.Authors: Victor Mauger-Vauglin, Jean-Emmanuel Migniau, Matthieu Guibert, Magali Loupias, Eric Daguisé, Alban Remillieux
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: update and numerical simulation of a cryostat for HARMONI AIT
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.  The Integral Field Unit (IFU) sub-system is part of an Integral Field Spectrograph cooled down to 130K. The IFU is in charge of splitting, slicing and rearranging the field of view into four long slits (~540mm) to feed four spectrographs. The alignment of each of the subsystems will be tested at 130K with our test cryostat upgraded to fit with the alignment control tools. This paper presents the thermal simulation of the current cryostat, fed by real tests data, in order to better estimate the thermal behaviour foreseen after its upgrade.

Items.Authors: C. Guillermo Gimenez de Castro, Carlos Francile, Fernando M. López, Tiago Giorgetti, Paulo J. Simões, Amauri S. Kudaka, Daniel R. de Sousa, Manuel G. Marciani, Gedeane G. Kenshima
Items.Title: HATS: a mid-IR photometer to investigate solar flares
Items.Abstract: We present the first mid-IR solar dedicated telescope to detect flares at the almost unexplored wavelength λ = 20 μm or 15 THz. The High Altitude THz Solar photometer (HATS) uses a thermally stabilized Golay cell as a detector and a bandpass filter to select the observing frequency. It is installed at 2350 m above sea level in the Andes Mountains (Argentina). HATS started the commissioning phase in April 2025. The main goal of the instrument is to comprehend the physical processes that occur during flares at chromospheric levels. HATS is part of several other instruments operated at CRAAM to observe solar flares at the IR to submillimeter wavelength range.

Items.Authors: Dan A. Kerley, Malcolm Smith, Edward Chapin, Jonathan Stocks, Lianne Mueller, Colin Richardson, Jean-Pierre Véran, Maaike van Kooten, Kate Jackson
Items.Title: HEART in action: supporting RTC development across many AO instruments and observatories
Items.Abstract: The Herzberg Extensible Adaptive Optics Real-time Toolkit (HEART) is a versatile software framework designed to support the development of AO RTCs. Developed by the National Research Council Canada - Herzberg Astronomy and Astrophysics Research Centre (NRC-HAA), HEART provides a modular collection of utilities and components and a scalable framework that enable efficient construction of RTCs across diverse AO systems. It is currently being used to build or design RTCs for several major AO system such as MORFEO and ANDES for ELT; GNAO, GPI2 and GIRMOS for Gemini; and NFIRAOS for TMT. HEART is also deployed on-sky in REVOLT at DAO. This paper highlights how HEART enables the construction of these distinct RTCs by reducing the need for extensive customization, while leveraging reusable components to enhance robustness, scalability, and development efficiency.

Items.Authors: Masato Kagitani, Keisuke Takahashi, Ryo Tsukui, Mikio Kurita, Yasuhiro Hirahara, Takeshi Sakanoi, Marcelo Emilio, Simone Daflon dos Santos, Kevin Lewis
Items.Title: High dynamic-range observation using a 1.8m off-axis telescope PLANETS: primary mirror polish and its support structures
Items.Abstract: We report the final figuring, profilometry, and support development of the PLANETS telescope primary mirror, a 1.8-m off-axis paraboloid. The surface figure was measured by the Dragging Three-Point Method (DTPM), which reconstructs the profile from local-curvature measurements by double integration. Straight, kagome-lattice, and circular paths were combined in the mirror coordinate system, and the final reconstructed figure error was 34 nm RMS within the 1740 mm clear aperture. High-spatial-frequency 2-mm-period tool marks produced by spiral polishing were evaluated using DTPM sag measurements and reduced from about 24 nm to 0.5 nm peak-to-valley by pitch lapping. We also developed active axial and lateral support systems: a 36-point whiffletree with active warping harnesses and a 24-point lateral support with active torque adjustment. These results demonstrate the feasibility of DTPM-based metrology, robot-arm-based figuring, and active support for a meter-class off-axis thin mirror.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Cabona, Francesco Canella, Riccardo Ciantini, Alessio Gambetta, Andrea Chiodini, Niccolò Barberio, Federico Capelli, Antonio Caruso, Serena Iacone, Paolo Laporta, Gianluca Galzerano, Stefania Stefani, Domenico Stranges, Adriano Ghedina, Emanuele Pace, Riccardo Claudi
Items.Title: High-Precision NIR absorption gas cell characterization for GIANO-B via broadband GHz dual-comb spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We present the filling procedure and the subsequent characterization of the two absorption gas cells (H and K bands) designed to enable high-precision wavelength calibration for GIANO-B spectrograph. The characterization of the reference cells was performed using dual-comb spectroscopy. Recent advances in GHz-repetition-rate optical frequency combs have enabled fast, broadband measurements, while software-based phase-noise compensation strategies have recently improved SNR performance when operating free-running combs. We measure the spectral features in the 1000–2400 nm range, with a spectral resolution of 1 GHz. The experiment uses two identical mode-locked lasers operating at ~1 GHz repetition rate, with a relative repetition-rate offset. The laser pulses are amplified, compressed, and spectrally broadened in new-generation Ta₂O₅ waveguides. Accurate wavelength referencing is provided by beating the comb with a narrow-linewidth CW laser in combination with an absolute wavemeter.

Items.Authors: Bryson Cale, Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, Max Brodheim, Ava DeLaGarza, Graham Bruce Berriman, Jeff Mader, Charlie Kilpatrick, James D. Neill, Samuel Halverson, Ben Sappey, Aidan Gibbs, Luke Finnerty, Quinn Konopacky, Ashley Baker, Charles Beichman, Rob Bertz, Jocelyn Ferrara, Michael Fitzgerald, Rose Gibson, Katelyn Horstman, Nem Jovanovic, Marc Kassis, Stephanie Leifer, Andrea Lin, Dimitri Mawet, Jason Wang
Items.Title: HISPEC data reduction pipeline I: architecture and calibration data management
Items.Abstract: We present the design of the Data Reduction Pipeline (DRP) for the upcoming HISPEC instrument at W. M. Keck Observatory which performs the science and calibration processing for HISPEC. The HISPEC DRP uses a modular object-oriented programing (OOP) structure where individual DRP steps, pipelines, and data model classes are straightforward to implement and configure. A key component of the DRP is an automated calibration file association and retrieval system. Calibration metadata are stored in a local SQLite database that is synced with a PostgreSQL database hosted at the Keck Observatory Archive (KOA). Calibration files are automatically associated and downloaded from KOA and cached locally for efficient reuse. The design of the HISPEC DRP and automated calibration system minimizes user-intervention and provides a robust, reproducible environment for processing and analyzing HISPEC data products.

Items.Authors: Oscar Gonzalez, Martin Black, Stephen Watson, Matteo Munari, Andrea Tozzi, Marco Riva, Sofia Randich, Andrea Bianco, Letizia Caito
Items.Title: HRMOS: a novel concept for a fibre positioner system with integrated ADC
Items.Abstract: HRMOS is a very high-resolution (R~80,000), multi-object (50-60) spectrograph, proposed as a new instrument for the VLT. HRMOS will address a broad range of transformative science questions. To achieve its science goals, one of the key technical challenges is that of atmospheric dispersion correction over the 25’ field of view of the VLT. One of the concepts being explored is to achieve this correction in the focal plane fibre positioning system, reducing the need for very large ADC opto-mechanics. In this paper, we present a novel concept for a traditional pick-and-place system (named QUACKS) that utilises configurable pick-off mirror units that are oriented prior to placement (named DUCKS). The ADC is done using optical receiver units placed around the edge of the telescope field (named ROCKS). The current opto-mechanical design of the developing concept, which can also be used by other future facilities, will be presented together with an overview of its benefits and challenges.

Items.Authors: Anna Brucalassi, Andrea Tozzi, Matteo Munari, Andrea Bianco, Simone D'Auria, Jose Schiappacasse Ulloa, José A. Araiza-Durán, Alen Khanbekyan, Manuela Arnò, Andrea Baruffolo, Martin Black, Emma Fernandez-Alvar, Michele Frangiamore, Oscar A. Gonzalez, Robert J. Harris, Enrique Jovén Álvarez, Graham J. Murray, Luis Rodríguez Ramos, Bernardo Salasnich, Letizia Caito, Enrico Giro, Laura Magrini, Maria Sofia Randich, Marco Riva, Sergio Sousa
Items.Title: HRMOS: towards the spectrograph design
Items.Abstract: The High-Resolution Multi-Object Spectrograph (HRMOS) is a facility instrument that we plan to propose for the Very Large Telescope (VLT) of the European Southern Observatory (ESO). HRMOS offers a combination of capabilities that are crucial for enabling breakthrough science across a wide range of active research fields, nucleo-cosmochronology, exoplanet studies, the origin of elements, and hierarchical galaxy assembly. It addresses a significant gap in the suite of instruments planned for the coming decade. The key features of HRMOS include high spectral resolution (R=80,000), multi-object capability (50-60 targets), and long-term stability, enabling considerable radial-velocity precision and accuracy (10 m/s). In this work, we present the ongoing development of the opto-mechanical design for a next-generation high-resolution spectrograph, with a focus on key engineering solutions implemented to fulfill the instrument demanding scientific requirements.

Items.Authors: Emiel H. Por, Mayra Gutierrez, Dan Sirbu, Rachel Morgan, Eduardo Bendek, Carson Valdez, Kevin Fogarty, Jordan Diaz, Laurent Pueyo
Items.Title: Hybrid photonic coronagraphy: integration and testing on the SEAL testbed
Items.Abstract: Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) can act as coronagraphs by routing telescope light through Mach–Zehnder interfermeter meshes whose phase shifters direct starlight away from the nulled channels. However, imperfections in the PIC limit performance. We investigate hybrid photonic coronagraphs that place a bulk-optic coronagraph upstream, suppressing most starlight before injection and substantially relaxing PIC tolerance requirements.    We test this concept by integrating a NASA Ames AstroPIC device into the UCSC SEAL testbed, performing free-space injection of focal-plane light using a microlens array aligned to on-chip grating couplers . We outline the prototype’s optical, mechanical, and thermal design and report initial throughput, contrast, and stability measurements, comparing direct and hybrid injection. These results probe the feasibility of hybrid photonic coronagraphy for next-generation high-contrast imagers for both ground- and space-based telescopes.

Items.Authors: Veronica Baldini, Giorgio Calderone, Roberto Cirami, Igor Coretti, Paolo Cucurullo, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Antonio Sulich, Ilaria Ermolli, Kamal Sant
Items.Title: IBIS 2.0 control system upgrade: from Dunn Solar Telescope to THEMIS
Items.Abstract: The Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) has been a key instrument for high-resolution imaging spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry at the Dunn Solar Telescope (DST, NSO, USA). As part of its relocation and upgrade to the THEMIS solar telescope (Tenerife, Spain), the instrument — now IBIS 2.0 — has undergone a complete redesign of its control electronics and software.  The new architecture is based on industrial Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) distributed across two dedicated control cabinets mounted near the instrument. This modular and robust configuration ensures precise coordination of all opto-mechanical subsystems, including the dual Fabry–Pérot interferometers, the polarization modulation unit, and the imaging cameras. The PLCs provide deterministic timing, precise motion control, and continuous status monitoring, while interfacing with high-level control software based on ESO VLT standards within the THEMIS observatory environment.

Items.Authors: Miguel Angel Gonzalez Bolivar, David Clarke, Nuria Lorente, Nuwanthika Fernando
Items.Title: ImageNinja: a python framework for modular data simulations
Items.Abstract: We created ImageNinja, a framework designed to build modular raw data simulations. Each simulation is driven by a series Python classes called Effectors. Each Effector replicates an aspect in the instrument’s data-generation process, from detector characteristics and external noise, to writing the raw data to FITS files. ImageNinja is designed to be instrument-agnostic, but its development has been focused on a specific instrument: the MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph (MAVIS). The current version of ImageNinja consists of three packages: CORE, FITS, and MAVIS. ImageNinja-CORE implements the main simulation framework, allowing users to plug in modules that perform the simulation steps. ImageNinja-FITS provides Effectors for the I/O of FITS files. Finally, ImageNinja-MAVIS contains the Effectors that replicate the data-collection process specific to MAVIS.

Items.Authors: Francesco Ceraudo, Giovanni Della Casa, Matias Antonelli, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Riccardo Campana, Ettore Del Monte, Evgeny Demenev, Giuseppe Dilillo, Yuri Evangelista, Marco Feroci, Francesco Ficorella, Mauro Fiorini, Edoardo Giancarli, Jacopo Giani, Marco Grassi, Giovanni Lombardi, Piero Malcovati, Filippo Mele, Alessio Nuti, Giancarlo Pepponi, Tonino Pisanu, Alexander Rachevski, Massimo Rapisarda, Irina Rashevskaya, Ajay Sharma, Marco Tambussi, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Yinhe Zhu, Nicola Zorzi, Francesca Esposito, Immacolata Donnarumma, Alessandro Turchi, Ugo Cortesi, Fabio D'Amico, Marco Gai, Andrea Argan
Items.Title: Imaging and spectroscopic performances of the detector assemblies for the lunar electromagnetic monitor in x-rays
Items.Abstract: The Lunar Electromagnetic Monitor in X-rays (LEM-X) is an Italian proposal for a Moon-based all-sky X-ray observatory, for the detection of transients and the long-term monitoring of sources in the 2-50 keV band, developed within the Earth Moon Mars project of the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Featuring a modular design, LEM-X is based on compact and lightweight coded-aperture cameras, each with a 2-sr field of view. The detector plane of each camera is built around four alumina-based Detector Assemblies (DAs), each one featuring a large-area (~7x7 cm2) Silicon Drift Detector (SDD), readout by CMOS analog Application Specific Integrated Circuits (AFE ASICs) named NOVA and specifically developed for this project. Four complete DAs, i.e. the full detector plane of one LEM-X caamera were developed and assembled. We will present the results of the performance tests demonstrating both the spectral and imaging capabilities of the devices.

Items.Authors: Caleb Cook, Nico Deshler, Logan Pawlowski, Amit Ashok
Items.Title: Imaging sub-diffraction star clusters with spatial mode sorting
Items.Abstract: Passive super-resolution imaging using spatial mode sorting has been vigorously analyzed as a technique to approach fundamental limits of resolution. However, a comprehensive experimental validation of this approach has been limited by the fidelity of hardware implementation of spatial mode sorters in terms of throughput, cross-talk, and spectral bandwidth. The recent availability of high-fidelity MPLC-based spatial mode sorters, such as those from Cailabs, enables a comprehensive experimental validation. In this work, we demonstrate sub-diffraction localization of point emitters, emulating star clusters, in various configurations and different spectral bandwidths. Our experiment employs a hybrid measurement method that combines direct imaging and spatial mode sorting measurements. Our measurement model and image estimation algorithm incorporates various error sources such as shot noise, detector dark current, read noise, residual wavefront error, and pointing error.

Items.Authors: Paul Rouquette, Benoît Neichel, Cédric Taïssir Héritier, Pierre Jouve, Anne Costille, Kjetil Dohlen, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: Impact of microlenses shape on the performance of laser guide star wavefront sensors for ELT-class telescopes
Items.Abstract: In this paper, the impact of the Shack-Hartmann microlenses on adaptive optics performances is characterized. To this end, an original approach combining microlens profile measurements, end-to-end simulations and experimental validation is proposed.

Items.Authors: Davide Savio, Ernesto Oliva, Alen Khanbekyan, Anna Brucalassi, Andrea Tozzi
Items.Title: Impact of modal noise on absolute wavelength calibration with fiber-fed laser frequency combs
Items.Abstract: Modal noise arising from fiber coupling can limit the accuracy of Laser Frequency Comb calibration in high-resolution spectrometers. We present experimental evidence showing how non-uniform fiber illumination leads to systematic wavelength distortions in individual calibration lines. While the impact on traditional radial velocity measurements based on the average of many spectral lines remains negligible, single-line wavelength determinations can be affected at the meter-per-second level. The effect depends strongly on modal excitation and can persist even in large-core fibres under under-filled illumination conditions, particularly when scrambling devices are used. These effects are particularly relevant for applications requiring accurate line-by-line wavelength comparisons, such as tests of the stability of fundamental constants. Understanding and mitigating modal noise is therefore essential for next-generation high-accuracy spectrographs and calibration systems.

Items.Authors: Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Hele I. Savin, Joonas K. M. Viuho, Gregory Bredthauer, Oskari Leiviskä, Seppo Mattila, Olli Setälä, Joseph Tufts, Ville Vähänissi, Petri Väisänen
Items.Title: Implementation of black silicon CCD for astronomical observations at the Nordic Optical Telescope
Items.Abstract: Nanostructured, or so-called "black'' silicon detectors can attain higher quantum efficiency and wider wavelength sensitivity range compared to traditional silicon CCD and CMOS sensors. These qualities are attractive for applications in low-light conditions such as in astronomical observations. We present the first concept of an instrument employing a black silicon CCD detector, planned to be mounted and tested at the Nordic Optical Telescope on the Canary Islands, Spain. In this paper, the preliminary design of the instrument and the plan for the implementation of the black silicon CCD chip in the instrument are described. Characterization and test plans for the instrument in both sea-level laboratory and mountaintop on-site conditions are discussed, followed by the utilization strategy of the instrument in actual astronomical observations.

Items.Authors: Haruka Suzuki, Itsuki Sakon, Takashi Onaka, Aoi Takahashi, Takafumi Ootsubo, Naofumi Fujishiro, Youichi Ohyama, Hideo Matsuhara
Items.Title: Improved data reduction procedure for the mid-infrared slit spectroscopy of AKARI/IRC LG2
Items.Abstract: In this presentation, we report on our technical efforts to evaluate and mitigate artifacts that have hindered accurate spectral extraction in AKARI Infrared Camera (IRC) LG2 slit spectroscopy. The AKARI/IRC LG2 slit spectroscopic data suffer from artifacts such as contamination by zeroth- and second-order light in the edge regions of the aperture mask, as well as scattered light produced by the incident beam within the field of view.    To establish a standardized procedure for deriving reliable LG2 slit spectra, we investigate the properties of the 0th, 1st, and 2nd order light, the slit properties, the geometry of the aperture mask, and the characteristics of the scattered light. Through these analyses, we develop a robust data-reduction method that eliminates previously uncorrected artifacts and enables accurate extraction of LG2 slit spectra, particularly for diffuse sources.

Items.Authors: Abhay Kumar, Sergio Fabiani, Ettore Del Monte, Giovanni Lombardi, Nicolas De Angelis, CUSP Collaboration
Items.Title: In orbit background for hard x-ray CubeSat polarimeters: case study of the CUSP mission in low-earth orbit
Items.Abstract: The CUbesat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP) project aims to measure the linear polarization of solar flares in hard X-ray band using a Compton scattering polarimeter. CUSP is a project in the framework of the Alcor Program of the Italian Space Agency.  As part of CUSP’s Phase B study, initiated in December 2024, optimizing the signal-to-background ratio is a key objective. In low-Earth orbit, the instrument is exposed to cosmic and albedo X-ray backgrounds, charged particles, and secondary radiation from the spacecraft and atmosphere. Simulating these contributions enables optimization of detector geometry and shielding to maximize signal-to-noise performance. This methodology provides a general framework for future CubeSat missions.    We present initial background estimates for CUSP using a GEANT4-based simulator. A detailed mass model of the CUSP has been implemented to simulate background components and estimated the background count rate in CUSP orbit.

Items.Authors: Riccardo Ferrazzoli, Enrico Costa, Sergio Fabiani, Philip Kaaret, Stephen L. O'Dell, Brian D. Ramsey, Paolo Soffitta, Luca Baldini, Ronaldo Bellazzini, Alessandro Di Marco, Fabio La Monaca, Luca Latronico, Alberto Manfreda, Fabio Muleri, John Rankin, Carmelo Sgrò, Stefano Silvestri, Martin C. Weisskopf
Items.Title: In-flight performance and stability of IXPE x-ray telescopes
Items.Abstract: We report a 30-month on-orbit assessment of IXPE’s three X-ray telescopes.   By fitting a composite PSF to point-source data and comparing with ground calibrations, we find stable imaging performance with mean HPDs of $26.1''$, $32.1''$, and $30.9''$ for Telescopes 1–3, respectively.   No secular degradation is seen, and count-rate effects are negligible up to ~60 cts s⁻¹ (2–3 keV).   A 99% C.L. upper limit of 4.4% is placed on optics-induced polarization in the PSF halo; the modulation factor shows no wing-to-core degradation.   IXPE meets its ≤30″ requirement and remains well suited for spatially resolved X-ray polarimetry through 2030.

Items.Authors: Alex Thomas, Bugao Zou, Shreya Sutariya, Yuhan Wang, Erin Healy, Claire Lessler, Jeffrey McMahon, Michael Niemack
Items.Title: Infrared blocking foam filters for millimeter-wave cameras
Items.Abstract: As the mechanisms governing the attenuation of IR-blocking foams used in Cosmic Microwave Background experiments were poorly understood, we present broadband (150 GHz to 1.5 THz) transmission spectroscopy of these foams, including Zotefoams (BICEP/Keck, SPT, CCAT, SO LAT) and Styroace-II (POLARBEAR, SO SATs). Our data are fit with a radiative transfer model incorporating Rayleigh scattering, Mie scattering, dielectric absorption, and higher-order scattering terms. We find that Zotefoams offer superior in-band transmission for mm and sub-mm bands. We also evaluate the tradeoff between Zotefoams, with lower densities offering increased transmission and decreased out-of-band attenuation. Finally, we estimate the scattering kernel and, therefore, the detector loading from blackbody radiation scattered at wide angles. In combination with our study of capacitive metal-mesh filters, we present quantitative recommendations for IR blocking filters for mm and sub-mm-wave observations.

Items.Authors: Andrew Shanahan, David Sheikh
Items.Title: In-orbit coated space telescope for FUV/EUV observation
Items.Abstract: ZeCoat is developing a new “commercial off-the-shelf” space telescope instrument, autonomously coated in the vacuum of space with bare aluminum to allow ultra-broadband observations, including select EUV bands. The baseline Cassegrain telescope design uses a 200-mm primary mirror made from 6061-aluminum alloy incorporating super-polished silicon-clad mirror surfaces, an EUV multilayer reflector, bare aluminum deposition once on-orbit, and black interference coatings for straylight suppression of baffle surfaces. The telescope complies with SmallSat mission constraints and can be tailored to operate from the EUV through RF wavelength bands. Larger telescope designs with primary mirrors up to 650-mm can currently be manufactured.

Items.Authors: Jean-Paul Breuer, Masato Yokota, Yasushi Fukazawa, Hiromitsu Takahashi, Jakub Řı́pa, Mariana Dafčíková, Filip Münz, Norbert Werner, Masanori Ohno, Balázs Csák, László Mészáros, András Pál, Marcel Frajt, Ján Hudec, Jakub Kapuš, Maksim Rezenov, Vladimír Dániel, Juraj Dudáš, Petr Svoboda, Hsiang-Kuang Chang, Chin-Ping Hu, Chih-Hsun Lin, Tsung-Che Liu, Kaustubha Sen, Che-Chih Tsao, Chih-En Wu, Hao Min Chang
Items.Title: Instrument response generation using high-resolution 3D voxilization of GRBAlpha and VZLUSat-2 satellites with MEGAlib
Items.Abstract: Pathfinder gamma-ray burst (GRB) detecting CubeSat missions such as GRBAlpha and VZLUSAT-2 have demonstrated the successful application of scintillator detectors with silicon photomultipliers in low Earth orbit (LEO). To produce more comprehensive scientific analysis of the data, the effective area of the detector needs to be characterised at different energies. A large part of this process requires a thorough understanding of the detectors response matrices based on the satellite mass model typically performed through Geant4 and MEGAlib simulations. We use a novel voxelization and binning methodology to turn complex 3D geometries into MEGAlib-compatible versions, and we validate these experiments by showing that the simulation results with Geant4 agree within an order of 10\%. We use MEGAlib simulations from various angles around the spacecraft to generate instrumental response matrices for both simple and complex geometries, in the case of GRBAlpha and VZLUSAT-2, respectively.

Items.Authors: Yoo Jung Kim, Michael P. Fitzgerald
Items.Title: Instrumental artifacts in photonic lantern spectroastrometry and their mitigation with PLred
Items.Abstract: Spectroastrometry is a powerful spectral-differential technique for probing angular scales below the diffraction limit, but it is well known to be susceptible to instrumental artifacts that can mimic or obscure real signals. In photonic lantern spectroastrometry, recently demonstrated on-sky with Subaru/FIRST-PL, the astrometric signal is encoded in relative flux variations between lantern outputs rather than in centroid shifts along a slit. This changes the artifact landscape: some slit-based spectroastrometric artifacts are avoided, but new artifact mechanisms emerge, including detector nonlinearity and spectral extraction errors, which can produce spurious features on emission or absorption lines. These lessons directly informed the design of PLred, an open-source Python package for photonic lantern data reduction and spectral-differential image reconstruction. We describe the origin of these artifacts and the key pipeline design choices used to mitigate them.

Items.Authors: Prakriti Gupta, Michael Langmayr, John I. Bailey, James D. Neill
Items.Title: InstrumentKit: a standard foundation for modern astronomical instrumentation
Items.Abstract: Modern astronomical instruments depend on increasingly capable and interconnected software systems. Developing an Instrument Control System (ICS) requires early decisions about architecture, interfaces, hardware integration, testing, deployment, documentation, and long-term operations while teams manage complex optical, mechanical, electrical, and scientific requirements.    InstrumentKit provides a standard software foundation for modern astronomical instrumentation. It offers reusable project scaffolding, refactorable design paradigms, hardware abstraction patterns, API foundations, testbed support, CI/CD workflows, and documentation templates. Rather than prescribing a single control system, InstrumentKit helps teams establish common foundations early while preserving flexibility for instrument-specific design.    By reducing repeated setup effort, InstrumentKit supports smoother development, easier onboarding, collaboration and long-term operations across the lifetime of an instrument.

Items.Authors: Pietro Ferraiuolo, Marco Bonaglia, Enrico Pinna, Azzaroli Nicolò, Luca Carbonaro, Giulia Carlà, Tommaso Lapucci, Paolo Spanò, Raffaele Tomelleri, Giovanni Negrini, Cristian Morando, Fabio Rossi, Matteo Menessini, Simone Esposito
Items.Title: Integration and alignment of the Petalometer testbench at INAF-Arcetri
Items.Abstract: Accurate phasing of segmented adaptive mirrors is a key requirement for achieving diffraction-limited performance on ELTs. Within the STILES project (PNRR), the INAF–Arcetri Adaptive Optics group is developing a dedicated petalometer testbench to evaluate phasing sensors for the ELT’s M4 mirror and GMT's M2. The bench integrates a six-segment “petalmirror,” each petal offering a 12 µm piston stroke, with internal metrology which will allow to measure the segment's relative piston with respect to the fixed central segment with nanometer accuracy. After completing hardware procurement, the team finalized acceptance measurements of the petalmirror and is now integrating the metrology system and the main optical relay—composed of the source unit and off-axis parabolas. The testbench will provide a controlled environment for validating phasing strategies for future ELT-class adaptive mirrors.

Items.Authors: Monde Manzini, Katlego Papane, Vhulahani Manukha, Evelyn Nkgadima
Items.Title: Integration and test facility effect towards operational SKA‑Mid telescope: a systems engineering approach
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array Mid-Frequency Telescope (SKA-Mid) is a massive, complex radio telescope system. To manage risks from its scale and digital complexity—where minor errors can cascade—the project employs a rigorous Systems Engineering approach. Central to this is an Integration and Test Facility (ITF) that serves as a high-fidelity digital twin and test environment. Using a specialized Sky Simulator as part of a Test Environment (TEnv), the ITF enables continuous verification of subsystems and core scientific performance in a controlled setting before deployment. This proactive strategy prevents costly on-site failures, ensuring the array meets its requirements and achieves operational resilience during the lifetime of the SKA-MId telescope. This paper outlines a systems engineering approach yielding a positive effect, risk mitigation and cost effective impact of having an ITF as a verification platform towards a successful commissioning and operation of the SKA-Mid telescope.

Items.Authors: Alessio Nuti, Edoardo Giancarli, Yuri Evangelista, Francesco Ceraudo, Giuseppe Dilillo, Riccardo Campana, Giovanni Della Casa, Ettore Del Monte, Marco Feroci, Mauro Fiorini, Giovanni Lombardi, Massimo Rapisarda, Francesca Esposito, Immacolata Donnarumma, Ugo Cortesi, Tonino Pisanu, Alessandro Turchi, Marco Gai, Andrea Argan
Items.Title: Internal alignment of the LEM-X coded-mask camera: classification of error contributions and impact on imaging performance
Items.Abstract: The Lunar Electromagnetic Monitor in X-rays (LEM-X) is a proposed all-sky X-ray observatory for the lunar surface, based on coded-aperture cameras each combining a coded mask and four large-area Silicon Drift Detectors. Imaging performance depends critically on the relative mask-detector alignment, which must be maintained under the operating conditions. We present a comprehensive analysis of the camera internal alignment budget: we classify the error contributions (manufacturing, long-term and short-term stability), their correctability, estimate the expected magnitude of each degree of freedom, and use end-to-end instrument simulation to quantify their impact on sensitivity, flux estimation, and source position. Comparison with the expected values shows the robustness of the design against the foreseen misalignments and provides quantitative guidance for its mechanical and thermal design.

Items.Authors: Andrea Lin, Ashley Baker, Sam Halverson, Nemanja Jovanovic, Dimitri Mawet, Garreth Ruane, Gautam Vasisht
Items.Title: Investigating the differential limb coupling effect for diffraction-limited spectrographs with PARVI
Items.Abstract: The upcoming HISPEC spectrograph for Keck II will use single-mode fibers fed by the telescope’s adaptive optics system, making it one of a handful of diffraction-limited spectrographs capable of precision radial velocities (PRVs). However, due to the target stars being partially resolved, the resulting RVs are predicted to be affected by differential limb coupling (DLC), where the red- and blue-shifted sides of the stellar disk are coupled unequally into the spectrograph across different epochs, producing an RV error term on the order of several m/s for nearby stars for HISPEC. We present our efforts to directly observe DLC on-sky for the first time with the diffraction-limited spectrograph PARVI in order to verify the expected behavior of DLC and subsequently develop mitigation strategies for HISPEC.

Items.Authors: Scott J. Lilley, Mahawa Cissé, Peter Wizinowich, Antonin Bouchez, Ed Wetherell, Eduardo Marin, Charlotte Guthery, Mitsuko Roberts, Nemanja Jovanovic
Items.Title: Keck near-infrared wavefront sensor adaptive optics (‘IWA): preliminary design
Items.Abstract: A near-Infrared Wavefront sensor Adaptive optics (‘IWA) system is being developed to optimize the Keck II Adaptive Optics (AO) system’s performance for science with the recently installed High order Advanced Keck Adaptive optics (HAKA) deformable mirror. ‘IWA will significantly enhance the performance and sky coverage delivered by the Keck II AO system to the existing ORKID imager and a suite of new science instruments: a mid-infrared coronagraphic integral field spectrograph (SCALES) and a fiber-fed high-resolution spectrograph (HISPEC).  We present the preliminary design of ‘IWA, focusing on the opto-mechanical design and the challenges of designing ‘IWA to fit within the limited space on the Keck II AO bench. We also present simulation results of the Keck II AO system’s performance with ‘IWA.

Items.Authors: Xiaojie Zhang, Haoran Yu, Jun Li, Yong Li, Cheng Liao, Yonghui Hou, Hangxin Ji
Items.Title: Key technologies for immersion systems in athermalized cameras of large optical telescopes: performance and stability evaluation of index matching fluids
Items.Abstract: This study evaluates five Cargille index-matching fluids (IMFs) for large-aperture athermalized immersion refractive cameras used in ground-based telescope spectrographs. Characterizations include refractive index measurement, material compatibility verification, and 1440-hour high-temperature accelerated aging. The tested IMFs exhibit distinct thermo-optic behaviors, with LL5610 showing stable negative responses and 1057B presenting nonlinear thermal variations. Fused silica and CaF2 achieve good compatibility, while specific optical glass and elastomers suffer obvious property changes. Fluid aging degradation is formulation-dependent. Slow filling inhibits bubbles but may cause uneven fluid distribution near lens defects. The results guide IMF selection, system optimization and practical engineering implementation for astronomical optical cameras.

Items.Authors: Shutaro Ueda, Yasuhiro Shoji, Daisuke Yonetoku, Tatsuya Sawano, Makoto Arimoto, Shoya Matsuda, Yoshiyuki Ando, Ryota Heibatake, Sohei Kawashima, Kaito Ozawa, Kimiyoshi Ichikawa, Norio Tokuda
Items.Title: KSAT3-X01: a 3U-size CubeSat mission for exploring charged particles in the Earth's magnetosphere with diamond detectors
Items.Abstract: We present a concept of the KSAT3-X01 project led by Kanazawa University. KSAT3-X01 is a 3U-size CubeSat mission planning for launch in 2027, aiming to explore charged particles in the Earth's magnetosphere with diamond detectors developed by Kanazawa University. Observations of charged particles, including electrons, protons, and ions, in the Earth's magnetosphere have revealed that an amount of charged particles is escaped from the Earth's magnetosphere. However, mechanism(s) to accelerate such particles remains unclear. In addition, it is challenging to measure the population of lower-energy particles at a few 10 keV. To address these problems, we have been developing our diamond detectors onboard KSAT3-X01. We measure the X-ray spectroscopic performance of the diamond detectors to evaluate signal charge corrections inside the diamond with several radioisotopes such as 241Am, 133Ba, and 109Cd. We find that our diamond detectors can detect X-rays above at least 10 keV.
